title: My partner won't go to therapy or admit there's a problem
summary: Your partner won't go to therapy, or says there's no problem? Why the ask lands as a verdict, what to try instead, and when the no is the answer.
body_markdown:
You finally said it out loud: "I think we should see someone." Maybe you'd rehearsed it for weeks. The answer came back fast. "We don't need therapy." Or "I'm not paying a stranger to tell me I'm a bad husband." Or the one that stings most: "What problem? We're fine."


Now you're holding two things at once. The original problem, which hasn't gone anywhere. And a new one: the person you'd need to fix it with won't agree it exists.


## A no to therapy and a no to the problem are different refusals


They often arrive in the same sentence. They mean different things, though, and they need different responses.


**"I don't want to go to therapy"** is usually a no to the format. Plenty of people who know something is off still balk at the office, the stranger, the bill, the hour of being examined. Some grew up in families where you didn't air things to outsiders. Some tried it once and couldn't stand the person. Some are quietly scared of what would come up. None of that means they don't care about the relationship.


**"There's no problem"** is a no to your experience. That one is harder, because it leaves you alone with something you can clearly feel while being told you're imagining it. If that's what happens every time you raise anything, it's worth reading about[what it does to you when your partner makes you feel crazy for bringing things up](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/my-partner-makes-me-feel-crazy) .


Before you push again, figure out which one you're hearing. A partner who says "I know things aren't great, I just don't want to do therapy" is giving you a lot more to work with than it feels like in the moment.


## Why the ask so often goes badly


Something we see a lot in Maia conversations: by the time someone asks their partner to go to therapy, they've usually been raising the problem for months, sometimes years, in smaller ways. Therapy is the last thing they can think of to try. So by the time they say it, they're frustrated, it's often in the middle of a fight, and it can sound like an ultimatum even if they don't mean it that way.


Their partner hears something different. You meant "I want us to get help." They heard "a professional is going to agree that you're the problem." Or "we're failing badly enough to need an emergency room." A lot of the time, the no is them defending themselves against that. People describe their partner reacting "like I'd suggested divorce," and from the other side, that may be close to how it felt.


That doesn't make the refusal okay. It does explain why asking the same way again, louder, rarely works.


## What to try instead of repeating the request


- **Talk about the problem, not the solution.** "I've been feeling really alone in the evenings and I don't know how to fix it" is easier to stay in the room with than "we need couples therapy." Agree on what's wrong first. The how comes later.
- **Put yourself in it too.** "I think I'm part of this and I want help figuring out my side" lowers the stakes. It's also usually true.
- **Shrink the ask.** One session, not a commitment. Or three, with a check-in afterward. A clear exit makes yes much cheaper to say.
- **Hand over some control.** Let them pick the therapist, the format (online feels less exposing to a lot of people), or the time. People resist less what they helped choose.
- **Ask what they'd do instead.** "Okay, not therapy. What do you think would actually help?" Then hold them to the answer. If it's "we'll just work on it," watch whether anything happens, because[agreeing to work on it and actually changing](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-said-wed-work-on-it-and-nothing-changed) are not the same thing.


## You're allowed to go on your own


Going alone can feel like admitting defeat, or like letting them off the hook. It's neither. Individual therapy gives you a place to get clear on what you want, what you're willing to accept, and what your own part in the pattern is. When one person starts showing up differently, the old moves stop working the same way, and that alone can move things more than another round of asking.


Some people find that once their partner sees them going, and sees it isn't a campaign to build a case, joining feels less threatening. That's not guaranteed, and it shouldn't be the secret goal. Go for you.


## When the no is the answer


If you've raised it gently, made the ask small, let them choose how, and they still won't go, won't suggest anything else, and won't acknowledge anything is wrong, the issue probably isn't your technique anymore. It's their willingness. That's painful. It's also information.


A relationship can survive a partner who hates therapy. It's a lot harder to get through with a partner who won't take part in fixing anything, by any route. If you've started to feel like[you're the only one trying](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/im-the-only-one-trying-in-my-relationship) , take that seriously, and give yourself room to ask the bigger question of[whether to keep trying at all](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-i-break-up-or-keep-trying) . You don't have to answer it today.


If you'd like somewhere to sort this out first (what exactly you're asking for, how to say it so it doesn't sound like blame, what you'll do if the answer stays no), you can talk it through with Maia. Get your thoughts straight before the next conversation, and come back to it after.
